title: The 34 km gap that sets your petrol price

scenes.narration: There is a 34 kilometre gap of water that decides what you pay for petrol. And right now, it is a war zone.
The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman. In a normal year, a fifth of the world's oil sails through here, around 20 million barrels a day. And a fifth of its liquefied gas.
On 28 February 2026, the US and Israel struck Iran. Iran's Revolutionary Guard answered by closing the strait. Ship traffic fell 70 percent overnight.
Then the attacks began. Tankers hit by missiles and drones. Mines laid in the shipping lanes. Within days, Indian seafarers were among the dead.
Within ten days, Brent crude crossed 100 dollars a barrel. By 19 March, Dubai crude hit a record 166.
Two thousand ships and twenty thousand sailors were trapped inside the Gulf. Insurers pulled out.
A ceasefire in April reopened it. Ten days later it closed again. A deal in June, broken in July. Each time, the tankers stopped.
Why does India care? We import about 90 percent of our crude oil, and nearly a third of it came through this strait.
So India rerouted. By March, 70 percent of its crude was being bought from outside the Gulf. And Iran now lets Indian ships through, for a fee.

elements.text: 70% of crude now sourced outside the Gulf
Indian ships allowed, for a fee

scenes.narration: This month, eleven ships were attacked in a single week. Three of them sank. Traffic is still 65 percent below normal.
Mediators are talking. Iran has seven demands. The US has its blockade. And every tanker that waits out here adds a few rupees to your fuel bill.
